evidence: Charis. p. 138; Diom. p. 326 P. (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The later grammarians’ term: verbum āctīvum, an active verb; genus āctīvum, the active voice (Traupman 245). For the grammarians an āctīvum verb was transitive, against neutra. Quintilian calls it faciendī modus, “the mode of doing” (see below).

terms.gloss: the active voice, “the mode of doing”
evidence: Quint. 9.3.7: et contrā faciendī quae patimur, ut vāpulō
terms.comment: Quintilian’s name, set against patiendī modus, the passive. The older name; the grammars and the classroom use the later one.

phrases.latin: in nātūrā verbōrum est et quae facimus patiendī modō saepe dīcere, ut arbitror, suspicor, et contrā faciendī quae patimur, ut vāpulō
phrases.english: it is in the nature of verbs often to say what we do in the passive, as arbitror, suspicor, and on the other hand in the active what we suffer, as vāpulō

phrases.latin: Cujus generis est? Āctīvī an passīvī? — Āctīvī.
phrases.english: What voice is it? Active or passive? — Active.

activus.html: From āctus, long by Lachmann’s law (Gell. 9.6.3), as āctiō.

sources: Lewis & Short: modus · Lewis & Short: activus
